sections.title: Operons: Prokaryotic Gene Organization (Contrast with Eukaryotic Genes)

blocks.x: A typical eukaryotic protein-coding gene is far more than just its coding sequence. Upstream of the transcription start site lies the promoter, a regulatory DNA region where RNA polymerase II and general transcription factors assemble. In many genes the promoter contains a TATA box (consensus TATAAT-like sequence, analogous in concept to the bacterial Pribnow box/−10 sequence), which positions the start of transcription; mutations in the TATA/Pribnow box can either decrease or increase promoter activity and generally affect the efficiency of transcription. Beyond the core promoter, enhancers can act at a distance (even from downstream or from within introns) to boost transcription, sometimes through mechanisms such as promoter or enhancer "addition," as occurs during immunoglobulin gene rearrangement in mammals where enhancer elements newly juxtaposed to a rearranged V(D)J segment activate its expression in B cells.
Split Genes: Exons, Introns, and Splicing

Most eukaryotic genes are "split genes" — their coding information (exons) is interrupted by non-coding intervening sequences (introns). Split genes were discovered independently by Phillip Sharp and Richard Roberts (in adenovirus, 1977; they shared the 1993 Nobel Prize, which is why exam questions sometimes cite "Sharp and Roberts (1993)" as the discovery reference). After transcription, the primary RNA transcript (pre-mRNA) undergoes splicing: introns are precisely excised and exons are joined together by the spliceosome, a large ribonucleoprotein complex built from small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) and associated proteins that recognize conserved splice-site sequences (the 5' GT and 3' AG dinucleotides that bound most introns, the "GT-AG rule," plus the branch-point adenosine). Alternative splicing of the same primary transcript allows a single gene to produce multiple protein isoforms.

The number of introns varies widely between genes — a fact tested directly in some quizzes (e.g., comparing globin, albumin, ovalbumin, and collagen genes, where the beta-globin gene classically has two introns interrupting three exons, versus other genes with many more or fewer). Genes are not always simple protein-coding, intron-containing units, either: heritable traits (both normal variation and disease) are shaped by protein-coding genes, RNA-coding genes (rRNA, tRNA, snRNA, miRNA, lncRNA genes, which are never translated), and epigenetic regulation (DNA methylation, histone modification) acting together — not coding sequence alone.

Because the genetic code is read in non-overlapping triplets (codons), a coding sequence has three possible reading frames in each direction; only one is normally used per exon/mRNA, and shifting it (see frameshift mutations below) scrambles the downstream code. Some genomic sequences resemble genes but are non-functional — pseudogenes are defined as defective, non-expressed copies of otherwise functional genes (often arising from gene duplication followed by degenerative mutation, or by retrotransposition of a processed mRNA lacking introns).

DNA replication is semiconservative: each of the two daughter double helices retains one original ("parental") strand and synthesizes one new strand, a mechanism proven by the classic Meselson-Stahl experiment. Key features and enzymes:

items: Helicase unwinds the parental double helix at the replication fork, breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs.

DNA polymerases synthesize new DNA strands 5'→3', always requiring a primer; they cannot initiate synthesis de novo. In prokaryotes, DNA polymerase III is the main replicative enzyme, while DNA polymerase I removes RNA primers and fills gaps (it also has 5'→3' exonuclease activity); DNA polymerase II is involved mainly in DNA repair, not the primary replicative machine.

Because the two parental strands are antiparallel and polymerase only synthesizes 5'→3', replication is continuous on the leading strand (synthesized continuously toward the fork) but discontinuous on the lagging strand, which is made as a series of short Okazaki fragments that are later joined by DNA ligase (after RNA primers are removed and replaced with DNA).

Replication occurs during the S phase of the cell cycle (not G1) — a frequently tested distractor, since G1 is the gap phase before DNA synthesis begins. Chromosome replication does not start with Okazaki fragment synthesis (that describes only lagging-strand synthesis, and even there, primer synthesis precedes it) — the defining, always-true statement about chromosome replication among typical exam options is simply that it is semiconservative.

Telomerase is a specialized reverse transcriptase that adds repetitive telomeric sequence to chromosome ends, compensating for the "end-replication problem" in which conventional DNA polymerases cannot fully replicate the very ends of linear chromosomes. Without telomerase, telomeres shorten with each division, contributing to replicative senescence/aging in most somatic cells; stem cells and neoplastic (cancer) cells characteristically reactivate/upregulate telomerase, giving them an extended or indefinite replicative lifespan.

A related exam fact: Taq polymerase, isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus, is heat-stable (active around 72°C, and its activity survives denaturation temperatures near 90–95°C), which is exactly why it is used in PCR — ordinary DNA polymerases would be destroyed by the repeated high-temperature denaturation steps.

blocks.x: A mutation is any heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of DNA. Mutations are the ultimate source of genetic variation and are essential for evolution, but classic multiple-choice items also stress that mutation alone does not directly create wholly new genes in the sense of instantly conferring new function (gene duplication plus subsequent divergence is generally invoked for the origin of new gene functions), and that processes like crossing-over and the resulting hybrid vigor (heterosis) are recombination phenomena, not mutations per se.

c: Base substitution that changes a codon but, due to redundancy (degeneracy) of the genetic code, still specifies the same amino acid

No change to primary protein sequence; however, silent changes are not always "invisible" — they can still have metabolic/phenotypic effects, e.g., by altering mRNA splicing signals, mRNA stability/folding, or the timing of co-translational protein folding (a point tested directly: "silent mutations have metabolic effect" = True)
Base substitution that changes the codon to specify a different amino acid

May be neutral (conservative substitution, little functional effect — e.g., Hb Bristol type changes), partially acceptable (e.g., sickle-cell hemoglobin, HbS, which is functional but pathological under certain conditions), or unacceptable/severely damaging (e.g., HbM variants causing methemoglobinemia) — i.e., missense mutations span a whole spectrum from harmless to lethal, so "point mutation can be all of the above (fully acceptable, partially acceptable, unacceptable)" is a valid composite answer
Base substitution that changes a sense codon into a stop codon (premature termination codon)
Produces a truncated, usually non-functional protein

blocks.x: Insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides not divisible by three shifts the reading frame downstream of the mutation, scrambling every subsequent codon. Frameshift mutations characteristically produce a completely non-functional ("useless") protein and very frequently generate a premature stop codon somewhere downstream — so the claim that a frameshift mutation "never results in premature chain termination" is false/incorrect (this is the kind of statement flagged as the wrong one in "which is incorrect" questions). Frameshift mutations are an important cause of human disease, including many forms of thalassemia (abnormal hemoglobin chain production due to frameshift or splice-site mutations in globin genes).
Substitution mutations are classified by the chemical nature of the base change:

items: Transition: a purine is replaced by the other purine (A↔G), or a pyrimidine by the other pyrimidine (C↔T). Transitions are generally more common than transversions because they are chemically favored by common mutational mechanisms (e.g., tautomeric shifts, deamination).
Transversion: a purine is replaced by a pyrimidine, or vice versa (e.g., A↔C, A↔T, G↔C, G↔T).

Radiation: X-rays and other ionizing radiation are mutagenic chiefly by breaking phosphodiester (phosphate ester) bonds in the DNA backbone, causing single- and double-strand breaks and chromosomal aberrations; H.J. Muller was the first to demonstrate the mutagenic effect of X-rays experimentally, using Drosophila (1927), work for which he later won the Nobel Prize. Non-ionizing UV radiation instead causes pyrimidine dimers (thymine dimers) that distort the DNA helix and block replication/transcription unless repaired.

Chemical mutagens act through several distinct mechanisms: base analogs (e.g., 5-bromouracil) get incorporated into DNA in place of a normal base and increase the rate of mispairing during replication; alkylating agents (e.g., ethyl methanesulfonate, nitrosoguanidine) add alkyl groups to bases, altering their pairing properties — nitrosoguanidine in particular is noted for acting preferentially at the DNA replication fork; intercalating agents (e.g., proflavin, ethidium bromide) wedge between stacked base pairs and typically cause frameshift mutations by distorting the helix during replication; deaminating agents (e.g., nitrous acid) remove amino groups from bases, converting cytosine to uracil (read as thymine) and adenine to hypoxanthine (read as guanine), thereby causing transition mutations. Deamination of cytosine, adenine, and guanine can all in principle alter base-pairing, but a subtlety tested in exams is that deamination of guanine specifically does not produce a heritable mutation under the typical scheme used in these questions (guanine deamination yields xanthine, which still base-pairs like guanine, unlike cytosine→uracil or adenine→hypoxanthine, which do change pairing specificity).

Biological mutagens: certain viruses, and parasitic fungi affecting crops (producing mycotoxins such as aflatoxin), are classic examples of naturally occurring mutagenic agents. Transposable elements ("jumping genes") can also cause mutations by inserting into or near genes, disrupting their sequence or regulation; replicative transposition (as seen with bacteriophage Mu, which integrates and replicates as part of its lifecycle) is one mechanism by which mobile elements propagate and mutate the genome.

Spontaneous mutation arises from multiple natural sources acting together: errors in DNA replication (misincorporation, slippage), spontaneous chemical changes such as depurination/deamination, imperfect DNA repair, and recombination — so "all of the above" is typically the correct composite answer for what causes spontaneous mutation. By contrast, hormonal imbalances are not considered a cause of mutation.

Mutagenicity testing: the Ames test is the standard assay for screening chemicals for mutagenic (and by extension, potential carcinogenic) potential, using histidine-auxotrophic Salmonella strains that revert to histidine prototrophy in the presence of a mutagen.

blocks.x: Germline vs. Somatic, Dominant vs. Recessive Mutations

items: Germinal (germline) mutations, occurring in egg or sperm-forming cells, are transmitted to offspring and are the cause of most genetically determined (heritable) diseases. Somatic mutations arise in non-germline body cells, are not passed to offspring, but can cause conditions like cancer within the individual (e.g., loss of heterozygosity at the retinoblastoma (RB1) locus can result from a chromosome loss, somatic mutation, or mitotic recombination — i.e., "all of the above" are valid mechanisms for the second, tumor-initiating hit).

Acquired mutations are, by definition, those that develop during an individual's lifetime (somatic mutations from environmental exposure, replication errors, etc.), as opposed to inherited germline mutations.

A recessive mutation is only phenotypically expressed in the homozygous state; a single copy in a heterozygote is typically masked (in the same generation, this means recessive mutations generally are not expressed unless homozygous — but they nonetheless can be detected if a mutant/homozygous individual is produced, so pedigree logic about "when is a germ-cell mutation detected" points to the next generation, once the mutant allele is inherited and potentially becomes homozygous).

A dominant autosomal mutation is expressed in heterozygotes: in a heterozygous (Aa) individual, 100% — not 50% — of that individual's own cells/phenotype show the trait (the classic "50%" answer in some question banks actually refers to the proportion of offspring from an Aa × aa cross who inherit the dominant allele and show the trait, so read these questions carefully for whether they ask about the individual or the next generation).

Marfan syndrome (an autosomal dominant connective-tissue disorder caused by mutations in the fibrillin-1/FBN1 gene) is a well-known example cited as a dominant-negative mutation, where the mutant protein product actively interferes with the function of the normal protein made from the other allele, rather than the disease resulting simply from a straightforward loss of half the normal gene dose.

Reversion (back mutation): a second mutation that restores (fully or partially) the original wild-type phenotype. The frequency of true reversion is generally low, so most single-nucleotide mutations are considered not readily reversible in practice, though reversion is documented in specific systems (e.g., somatic reversion producing patches of normal skin in Bloom syndrome, a chromosome-instability disorder).

blocks.x: Beyond changes to individual nucleotides, mutations can involve larger rearrangements of chromosome structure:

items: Deletion: loss of a chromosomal segment (e.g., 5p− in cri-du-chat syndrome). Visible cytologically in specially prepared tissues as deletion loops in the giant polytene chromosomes of dipteran salivary glands, where the normal homolog loops out opposite the deleted segment during pairing.

Duplication: a segment is present in extra copy. Generally considered less harmful than a comparable deletion, because duplications add genetic material (and thus rarely eliminate essential gene function) rather than removing it, whereas deletions can unmask recessive alleles on the homologous chromosome or remove essential genes entirely.

Inversion: a segment is excised, flipped 180°, and reinserted; classified as paracentric (does not include the centromere) or pericentric (includes the centromere). Inversion carriers are typically clinically normal themselves (an inversion, by itself, usually does not directly disrupt gene dosage), but they are at increased reproductive risk: crossing-over between homologs within the inverted region during meiosis produces unbalanced gametes (with duplications and deletions), so inversion carriers do carry an elevated risk of chromosomally unbalanced offspring even though the carrier is often phenotypically unaffected. Inversions have also been documented as a form of gene expression control in bacteria and bacteriophages (e.g., invertible DNA segments controlling flagellar-phase variation in Salmonella, and similarly documented in Neurospora and Drosophila contexts in some question banks).

Translocation: exchange of segments between non-homologous chromosomes (reciprocal translocation) or fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes (Robertsonian translocation, relevant to some familial Down syndrome cases). A translocation carrying an X-linked recessive gene onto an autosome, or an X-autosome translocation, can occasionally allow an X-linked recessive trait to be expressed in a female carrier — because the normal X may become preferentially inactivated in cells carrying the translocation.
Crossing-over occurring both within and outside an inverted region can generate a range of secondary deletions and duplications in the resulting recombinant chromosomes.

Cytogenetic banding techniques (e.g., R-banding, which stains the reverse pattern from standard G-banding) are used to detect chromosome polymorphisms, minor deletions, and inversions/rearrangements — i.e., banding is a general-purpose tool for identifying a broad range of structural chromosome changes, not just one category.

blocks.x: Cells possess multiple DNA repair pathways to correct damage before it becomes a fixed mutation, including mismatch repair (corrects replication errors missed by proofreading), base excision repair (removes damaged single bases, e.g., deaminated or oxidized bases), nucleotide excision repair (removes bulky lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers), and double-strand break repair (homologous recombination and non-homologous end joining). Defects in these pathways cause distinct human syndromes, several of which are commonly tested: Cockayne syndrome (a nucleotide-excision-repair-linked disorder in which UV-induced DNA damage is not properly repaired, producing premature aging and dwarfism; it is inherited in an autosomal recessive, not dominant, manner — a frequently flagged exam trap) and Bloom syndrome (defective BLM helicase, leading to genomic instability and a documented capacity for phenotypic reversion via back mutation, as noted above).

Not all inheritance follows Mendelian nuclear rules. Mitochondria (and, in plants, chloroplasts) contain their own small, circular, "naked" (histone-free) DNA genomes and are semi-autonomous organelles that generate ATP (mitochondria via oxidative phosphorylation; chloroplasts via photosynthesis) — a shared feature examined directly ("what is common between mitochondria and chloroplasts" = naked DNA, semi-autonomous nature, and ATP production, i.e., all of the above).

items: Maternal inheritance: because the egg contributes essentially all of the cytoplasm (and hence all the mitochondria) to the zygote, while sperm contribute almost none, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) traits are transmitted only through the mother. An affected mother passes the trait to all her children (sons and daughters), but only her daughters transmit it further; affected fathers do not transmit mtDNA traits to any offspring. Importantly, however, maternal inheritance does not always indicate extranuclear (cytoplasmic) inheritance — some nuclear-encoded traits can also show a maternal-effect inheritance pattern (where the mother's own nuclear genotype, not her cytoplasm per se, determines offspring phenotype), so the two concepts should not be treated as identical.

mtDNA and lineage tracing: because mtDNA is maternally transmitted, it is used to trace maternal lineages — and this technique can be applied to trace the maternal ancestry of both men and women (everyone inherits their mother's mtDNA, regardless of their own sex; only females pass it on further).

mtDNA has a distinctive buoyant density (generally lower than nuclear DNA in many organisms, related to its base composition and lack of associated histones) and, notably, mitochondria have limited/inadequate DNA repair capacity compared to the nucleus, making mtDNA more vulnerable to accumulating mutations over a lifetime — contrary to any assumption that it is somehow protected from mutation.

Mitochondrial disease examples: Kearns-Sayre syndrome (progressive external ophthalmoplegia, retinopathy, cardiac conduction defects) is caused by a large-scale deletion of a portion of mitochondrial DNA. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (Leber's blindness) is caused by a point mutation in mitochondrial DNA (commonly affecting complex I genes of the respiratory chain). Historically, 1988 is cited as the year the first disease-causing mitochondrial DNA mutation was reported (in the same period, both Kearns-Sayre-associated deletions and the first LHON point mutation were described). Other conditions linked to mitochondrial DNA changes/dysfunction discussed in this context include chronic (progressive external) ophthalmoplegia and associations proposed with neurodegenerative conditions such as Parkinson's disease.

Historical foundations of cytoplasmic inheritance: the phenomenon was pioneered by researchers including Correns (variegation in four-o'clock plants, an early demonstration of non-Mendelian, maternally transmitted inheritance) and Ephrussi (petite mutants in yeast, linked to mitochondrial dysfunction) — these two names are classically paired as founders of cytoplasmic inheritance studies, distinct from nuclear-inheritance pioneers such as Mendel, Morgan, and Bridges (who are instead associated with classical chromosomal/Mendelian mutation genetics, alongside Hugo de Vries, who first coined the term "mutation").

sections.title: Operons: Prokaryotic Gene Organization (Contrast with Eukaryotic Genes)

blocks.x: Although this topic centers on eukaryotic gene structure and mutation, exam banks frequently pair it with prokaryotic operon organization as a point of contrast. An operon is a cluster of coregulated structural genes under the control of a single promoter and operator, functioning as one transcriptional unit — importantly, the genes within an operon do not always need to share obvious functional relationships to be co-transcribed, though most do share a metabolic pathway. Operons are far more common in prokaryotes than in "higher" eukaryotic organisms (eukaryotic genes are typically transcribed individually, each with its own promoter); a rare and specifically tested exception is Caenorhabditis elegans, one of the few eukaryotes known to organize some genes into operon-like polycistronic units.

items: The lac operon (lactose metabolism in E. coli) is regulated by multiple interacting factors: the availability of lactose (inducer) and of glucose (via catabolite repression, involving cAMP and CAP), making "all of the above/many factors" the accurate composite description of its control. Mutations in lacZ (β-galactosidase) or lacY (permease) can each independently produce a Lac⁻ phenotype (cells unable to utilize lactose), since both gene products are required for effective lactose uptake and breakdown; lacA (transacetylase) mutants, by contrast, do not block lactose utilization.

The trp operon (tryptophan biosynthesis) is a classic example of a repressible operon under negative control: when tryptophan is abundant, it acts as a corepressor, activating the repressor protein to bind the operator and shut down transcription — the opposite regulatory logic from the inducible lac operon.

Positive control (where a regulatory protein must actively bind to activate transcription, rather than simply being removed to permit it) is characteristic of inducible operons for several sugars in some bacteria, including arabinose, maltose, and (via CAP/cAMP) lactose and galactose systems — commonly summarized in exam banks as "all of these" require positive control elements for full expression.

Regulatory architecture: a regulator gene produces a repressor/regulatory protein that controls the operator (the DNA site the repressor binds), which in turn controls transcription of the downstream structural genes; genes needed constantly for basic cellular function, largely independent of this kind of regulation, are called housekeeping genes. The gene encoding DNA-dependent RNA polymerase itself is not considered part of any specific operon it transcribes — it is a separate, independently regulated (typically constitutive/housekeeping-like) gene.
